quote: Nothing but a breath—a comma—separates life from life everlasting. It is very simple really.
source: Margaret Edson, attributed: Wit, the Donne flashback, pp. 14 to 15 (E. M. Ashford) (Faber and Faber, 1999)
speaker: E. M. Ashford
note: The line is Edson’s, spoken by E. M. Ashford in Wit. The wording comes from a study guide keyed to pages 14 and 15 of the Faber and Faber edition of 1999. The printed page was not opened, and one other secondary source gives the second sentence as Very simple, really.

evidence.where: LitCharts quotation pages for Wit (quotes page and the E. M. Ashford character page), both citing pp. 14 to 15 with this exact wording; corroborated in first sentence by several reviews. The two archive.org scans of the Faber and Faber 1999 edition (witplay00edso, wit00marg) are lending copies whose text could not be searched. Note and Query (2014) prints the passage as Nothing but a breath, a comma, separates life from life everlasting. . . . Very simple, really.
evidence.edition: Wit: A Play, Faber and Faber, New York, 1999 (not opened)
evidence.locator: the flashback in which Professor E. M. Ashford corrects the student Vivian Bearing on the punctuation of Death be not proud, pp. 14 to 15

reason: Authorship, play and speaker are certain and the play was published in 1999, inside scope, but the trail for the exact wording ends in a study guide and the secondary sources disagree on the second sentence. Under the standard that is a hedge until someone reads page 15 of the Faber text; the first sentence alone is the safer cut if the editor prefers.
